analysis.one_liner: Removes the legal shield that protects government officials from lawsuits when they violate constitutional rights.
analysis.headline: The bill never left the Senate Judiciary Committee: introduced July 1, 2020, it was referred to committee and received no further action before the 116th Congress ended in January 2021.
analysis.plain_summary: When a government official — most often a police officer — violates someone's constitutional rights, a judge-made rule called "qualified immunity" blocks the victim from winning damages unless the exact right was already "clearly established" in prior cases. This bill would amend the 1871 civil rights statute so that good faith or an unclear legal landscape could no longer be used as a defense. Victims of police misconduct and other official abuses could again sue for damages, as they could under the original law for its first century.
analysis.who_benefits: People whose constitutional rights are violated by state and local officials — especially victims of police misconduct, whose lawsuits are currently dismissed under qualified immunity before the merits are ever heard.

how_it_helps.text: Restores the ability to win damages under 42 U.S.C. 1983 even when a right was not "clearly established" at the time of the violation, reversing limits the Supreme Court layered onto the 1871 statute in 1967 and 1982. [S2] [S3]
Explicitly bars three defenses courts currently accept: that the official acted in good faith, believed the conduct was lawful, or could not reasonably have known the law. [S2] [S3]
The bill's findings state the doctrine has "severely limited" recovery for plaintiffs and frustrated Congress's original intent in passing the 1871 Ku Klux Klan Act. [S3]

analysis.who_pays: Government officials who violate constitutional rights would face personal liability for damages, and state and local governments would face more lawsuits, litigation costs, and higher insurance and settlement expenses paid ultimately by taxpayers.

drawbacks.text: State and local governments would absorb more litigation costs and larger payouts, which fall on taxpayers and could strain small municipal budgets. [S2] [S3]

Removing the good-faith defense entirely means an officer who reasonably but mistakenly believed the law allowed their conduct could still be personally liable — a strong objection from law enforcement, which argues this would make split-second decisions unworkably risky. [S2]
Opponents argue broader liability could deter qualified people from serving as police officers or other government employees. [S2]

analysis.benefit_vs_cost: For the people whose rights are violated, the benefit is real: today most such lawsuits are thrown out without ever reaching the question of whether the conduct was wrong. The costs are genuine too — more litigation and liability for governments — but the bill addresses a one-way shield that currently lets officials violate rights with no damages consequence at all, while criminal prosecution remains rare.

outcome.mechanism: It sat in the Senate Judiciary Committee from July 2020 until the Congress ended in January 2021; the committee never acted on it and the Senate never voted on it.

narrative.text: Sen. Markey, joined by Sens. Sanders and Warren, introduced the bill on July 1, 2020. [S1] [S4]
It was read twice and referred to the Senate Judiciary Committee the same day. [S5]
That referral was the final action of record; no hearing, markup, or floor vote ever followed before the 116th Congress expired. [S5]

outcome.who_came_out_ahead: Government officials — police officers in particular — and the municipalities that back them keep the qualified immunity shield, and victims of rights violations remain unable to recover damages. Short: Government officials keep their immunity shield.

analysis.who_came_out_ahead_short: Government officials keep their immunity shield

for.name: Sen. Elizabeth Warren
for.role: Cosponsor; handled the introduction on the floor
for.what_they_did: Cosponsored the bill and introduced it on behalf of Markey, Sanders, and herself.

against.name: Sen. Lindsey Graham
against.what_they_did: Never scheduled committee action on the bill after it was referred to Judiciary on July 1, 2020; the referral was the bill's last action of record.

against.name: Sen. Mitch McConnell
against.what_they_did: Never brought the bill to the Senate floor for a vote during the remainder of the 116th Congress.

sides.party_line_note: Only three senators backed it, all aligned with Democrats (one Independent), and the Republican majority never moved it; no vote was ever recorded, so no official party split exists.

industries.industry: Law enforcement officers and police unions
industries.note: The bill removes the personal liability shield that protects officers from damages suits when courts find constitutional violations. Police unions opposed ending qualified immunity, and their resistance is the principal reason reform stalled in both chambers of Congress.
Municipalities would face more civil rights lawsuits, larger settlements, and higher insurance costs as the party ultimately covering officer misconduct. Governments argued this would strain budgets.
More litigation and higher payouts translate into larger premiums for the insurers that cover municipalities and officials, paid out of local government budgets.
